title: Searching
html:
Advanced searching is rarely “find x in a sorted array”. It is recognising that a problem has a monotone structure — an index range that can be halved, an answer range that can be halved, or two ends that can be walked inwards — and then applying binary search or two pointers to it.

Binary search (general form) — given a predicate that is false for a prefix of the search space and true for the rest, find the boundary in O(log n) probes. Searching for a value in a sorted array is just the special case arr[i] >= x.

The four patterns in this topic

Binary search on an index

The array is sorted, or piecewise sorted (rotated, bitonic). Decide in O(1) which half can contain the answer and discard the other.

Binary search on the answer

The array is not sorted, but the answer is a number and “is ans feasible?” is monotone. Binary search over the answer range, checking feasibility in O(n).

Two pointers

One pointer at each end of a sorted array; the sum tells you which pointer to move. Pair / triplet with a given sum.

Cycle detection on indices

Treat i → arr[i] as a linked list. Floyd's tortoise-and-hare finds the repeated value in O(n) time and O(1) space without touching the array.

ProblemPatternTimeExtra space
Search in an infinite sorted arraydoubling + binary searchO(log p) (p = position)O(1)
Search in a sorted rotated arraybinary search with a sorted-half testO(log n)O(1)
Find a peak elementbinary search towards the rising sideO(log n)O(1)
Pair with given sum (sorted)two pointersO(n)O(1)
Triplet with given sum (sorted)fix one + two pointersO(n²)O(1)
Median of two sorted arraysbinary search on a partitionO(log min(n1, n2))O(1)
Repeating elementFloyd's cycle detectionO(n)O(1)
Allocate minimum pagesbinary search on the answerO(n log S)O(1)
Key point

Every solution below uses the same loop skeleton: while low <= high: mid = low + (high - low) // 2 … with low = mid + 1 or high = mid - 1. Writing low + (high - low) / 2 instead of (low + high) / 2 avoids integer overflow in C++ and Java when low + high exceeds 2³¹ - 1.

Search in an infinite sorted array

Example

Input: arr = [10, 15, 20, 40, 80, 80, 90, 100, 120, …], x = 100
Output: 7
Input: arr = [10, 15, 20, 40, 80, 80, 90, 100, 120, …], x = 50
Output: -1

The array has no known size (think of a stream, a file, or an API that returns elements by index), so high = n - 1 is unavailable. A linear scan is O(p) where p is the position of x. We can do better: find a bracket around x first.

Idea

Double the index until arr[i] >= x: probe 1, 2, 4, 8, …. After O(log p) probes we know x lies in (i/2, i], a range of size i/2. One binary search on that range finds it in another O(log p) steps.

1
Check index 0
If arr[0] == x return 0.
2
Gallop
Start at i = 1; while arr[i] < x set i = 2i. Stop when arr[i] >= x (or we have overshot into values larger than x).
3
Binary search
Search for x in [i/2 + 1, i] — every index below i/2 + 1 was already seen to be < x.

The efficient version only needs at(i) — a way to read the element at position i. The demo below models the infinite array with a function that returns a very large value beyond the data we actually have, which is exactly how a real stream would look (“everything further out is bigger than anything we are searching for”).

Time O(log p)Space O(1)
Key point

p is the position of x, not the (unknown) array size. The same “gallop then binary search” trick is exponential search; Timsort uses it to merge runs of very different lengths.

Search in a sorted rotated array

Example

Input: arr = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 8, 9], x = 30
Output: 2
Input: arr = [100, 200, 300, 10, 20], x = 40
Output: -1

A sorted array rotated by some unknown amount consists of two sorted runs, with the second run entirely smaller than the first. Plain binary search fails because arr[mid] < x no longer tells you which side x is on.

Idea

At every step one of the two halves is sorted — if arr[low] < arr[mid] the left half is, otherwise the right half is. Check whether x lies inside the sorted half (a simple range test); if yes, search there, otherwise search the other half. Each step still discards half the array.

Time O(log n)Space O(1)
Pitfall

Use arr[low] <= arr[mid] (not <) so that a two-element window like [8, 9] with mid == low is classified as “left half sorted”. The original notes used <, which sends x = 8 the wrong way in such windows. With duplicates ([3, 1, 3, 3, 3]) neither half can be identified and the worst case degrades to O(n).

Find a peak element

Example

Input: arr = [5, 10, 20, 15, 7]
Output: 20
Input: arr = [10, 20, 15, 5, 23, 90, 67]
Output: 20 (90 is also a valid answer)

A peak is an element that is not smaller than its neighbours (the ends only have one neighbour). Every array has at least one peak — the maximum is always one — but we only need any peak, which is what makes O(log n) possible.

Idea

Look at mid. If it is a peak, done. If its left neighbour is bigger, the left half must contain a peak: walking left along rising values must eventually stop, either at a local maximum or at index 0 — both are peaks. Symmetrically, if the right neighbour is bigger, go right.

Time O(log n)Space O(1)
Key point

The array is not sorted here — binary search works because the predicate “a peak exists in this half” can be decided from mid and one neighbour. The same reasoning finds the maximum of a bitonic array (strictly increasing then strictly decreasing).

Two-pointer approach: pair with a given sum

Example

Input: arr = [2, 5, 8, 12, 30], x = 17
Output: true
Input: arr = [3, 8, 13, 18], x = 14
Output: false

Given a sorted array, is there a pair whose sum is x? The brute force tries all n(n-1)/2 pairs.

Idea

Put i at the start and j at the end. If arr[i] + arr[j] < x the sum must grow — only moving i right can do that (every pair with this i and a smaller j is even smaller, so i is finished). If the sum is too large, move j left. Each step retires one index, so at most n steps.

Time O(n)Space O(1)
Key point

If the array is not sorted, two pointers need an O(n log n) sort first; a hash set gives O(n) time with O(n) space instead (see Hashing). Two pointers win when the input is already sorted or when O(1) extra space is required.

Triplet in a sorted array

Example

Input: arr = [2, 3, 4, 8, 9, 20, 40], x = 32
Output: true
Input: arr = [1, 2, 5, 6], x = 14
Output: false

Idea

Fix the smallest element arr[i] of the triplet, then ask the two-pointer routine for a pair with sum x - arr[i] in the suffix arr[i+1..]. Searching only to the right avoids reusing arr[i] and avoids counting the same triplet three times. n fixes × O(n) pair search = O(n²), down from the O(n³) triple loop.

Time O(n²)Space O(1)
Key point

This is the standard 3-Sum technique. To list all distinct triplets instead of answering yes/no, skip over equal values after each move of i, j and the fixed index so duplicates are not reported twice.

Median of two sorted arrays

Example

Input: a1 = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50], a2 = [5, 15, 25, 35, 45]
Output: 27.5
Input: a1 = [1, 2, 3], a2 = [4, 5, 6]
Output: 3.5
Input: a1 = [1, 3, 5], a2 = [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]
Output: 4.5

The median of the merged array is wanted, without merging. Merging takes O(n1 + n2) time and space; the target is O(log min(n1, n2)).

Idea

The median splits the n1 + n2 elements into a left half and a right half of (almost) equal size. Take i1 elements from a1 and i2 = (n1 + n2 + 1) / 2 - i1 from a2 to form the left half. The split is correct exactly when every left element is <= every right element: maxLeft1 <= minRight2 and maxLeft2 <= minRight1. If maxLeft1 > minRight2, i1 is too big — binary search i1 over [0, n1].

1
Make a1 the shorter array
Swap if needed, so the search space is [0, n1] with n1 = min, and i2 always stays within [0, n2].
2
Binary search i1
i1 = (low + high) / 2, i2 = (n1 + n2 + 1) / 2 - i1. Use -∞ / +∞ when a side of a split is empty.
3
Check the partition
maxLeft1 <= minRight2 and maxLeft2 <= minRight1 → found. If maxLeft1 > minRight2 move high = i1 - 1, else low = i1 + 1.
4
Read the median
Odd total: max(maxLeft1, maxLeft2). Even total: average of that and min(minRight1, minRight2).

To keep the four programs' output byte-identical the code computes twice the median as an integer (the sum of the two middle values) and prints it as k.0 or k.5 — the median of integers is always a whole or half number.

Time O(log min(n1, n2))Space O(1)
Pitfall

Three bugs in the original notes, all fixed above: maxLeft1 for an empty left part must be -∞, not +∞; a2[i2] and a2[i2 - 1] need the same empty-side guards as a1, otherwise i2 == n2 indexes out of range; and the solution assumed len(a1) <= len(a2) without enforcing it. Also the notes' answer for [1, 3, 5] and [2, 4, 6, 8, 10] was 4.0 — the merged array is 1 2 3 4 5 6 8 10, so the median is 4.5.

Repeating element

Constraints that make this problem interesting:

  • array size n >= 2
  • exactly one value repeats — any number of times
  • all values from 0 to max(arr) are present, so 0 <= max(arr) <= n - 2
Example

Input: arr = [0, 2, 1, 3, 2, 2]
Output: 2
Input: arr = [1, 3, 2, 4, 3, 3]
Output: 3

ApproachTimeExtra spaceModifies array?
Compare every pairO(n²)O(1)no
Sort, then compare neighboursO(n log n)O(1)yes
Hash set of seen valuesO(n)O(n)no
Boolean visited array (values are < n)O(n)O(n)no
Floyd's cycle detection on i → arr[i]O(n)O(1)no

Because every value is smaller than n, a boolean array indexed by value replaces the hash set — same O(n) time, less constant overhead, no hashing.

Time O(n)Space O(n)

Repeating element in O(n) time, O(1) space, array unchanged

Example

Input: arr = [0, 2, 1, 3, 2, 2]
Output: 2
Input: arr = [1, 3, 2, 4, 3, 3]
Output: 3
Input: arr = [0, 0]
Output: 0

Now the array may not be modified and no extra array is allowed. The trick is to stop looking at the values as data and treat them as pointers.

Idea

Define next(i) = arr[i] + 1. Index 0 is never anybody's next (values are >= 0, so next >= 1), and every index has exactly one outgoing edge — the structure is a linked list that ends in a cycle (a ρ shape), starting at 0. The repeated value is the node with two incoming edges, which is precisely where the cycle begins. Floyd's tortoise-and-hare finds that node in O(n) with two integer variables; subtract the +1 to recover the value.

1
Phase 1 — meet inside the cycle
slow = next(slow), fast = next(next(fast)) from 0 until they are equal. They must meet because once both are on the cycle the gap shrinks by one every step.
2
Phase 2 — find the entry
Reset slow = 0; move both one step at a time. They meet exactly at the cycle entry (the distance from 0 to the entry equals the distance from the meeting point to the entry, modulo the cycle length).
3
Recover the value
The entry index is v + 1 for the repeated value v, so return entry - 1.
Time O(n)Space O(1)
Pitfall

The +1 shift matters. Without it, arr[0] == 0 makes index 0 point to itself and the “start” is already inside a cycle, so Floyd's phase 2 returns the wrong node. The popular variant Find the Duplicate Number (n + 1 values in 1..n) needs no shift because its values are already >= 1 — use next(i) = arr[i] and return the entry itself. The notes' example [1, 1] belongs to that variant (it violates max(arr) <= n - 2), so it was replaced by [0, 0].

Allocate minimum number of pages

Example

Input: pages = [10, 20, 30, 40], k = 2
Output: 60
Input: pages = [10, 20, 30], k = 1
Output: 60
Input: pages = [10, 20, 30, 40], k = 3
Output: 40

n books with pages[i] pages must be split among k students. Each student gets a contiguous run of books and every book goes to someone. Minimise the maximum number of pages any one student reads. For [10, 20, 30, 40] and k = 2 the best split is [10, 20, 30] | [40] → max(60, 40) = 60.

The recursion explores C(n-1, k-1) ways of placing cuts. Memoising it gives an O(n² k) dynamic programme — still slow. The breakthrough is to search over the answer instead of over the cuts.

Idea

Ask the inverse question: “can every student stay within cap pages?” Greedily fill students left to right; start a new student whenever adding the next book would exceed cap. If at most k students were needed, cap is feasible. Feasibility is monotone — a larger cap is never harder — so binary search the smallest feasible cap between max(pages) (one book must fit) and sum(pages) (one student takes all).

1
Bounds
low = max(pages), high = sum(pages). The answer is always in this range.
2
Probe
mid = (low + high) / 2. Run the greedy isFeasible(mid) in O(n).
3
Shrink
Feasible → record mid, try smaller (high = mid - 1). Not feasible → low = mid + 1.
Time O(n log S), S = sum of pagesSpace O(1)
Key point

Binary search on the answer is a template worth memorising: Split Array Largest Sum, Painter's Partition, Koko Eating Bananas, Capacity to Ship Packages, Aggressive Cows and Minimum Days to Make Bouquets are all “smallest (or largest) value for which a greedy O(n) check passes”. The two things to get right are the bounds and the direction of monotonicity.

Pitfall

The notes' isFeasible read n from a global variable and the naive solution summed slices inside the loop (O(n) per cut). Also note k > n is impossible to satisfy if every student must receive a book — decide and document that edge case before coding.

Interview Q&A

When can binary search be applied to an unsorted array?

Whenever there is a predicate over positions that is false … false true … true (monotone), or a way to tell from O(1) local information which half must contain an answer. Peak finding (compare mid with a neighbour) and rotated-array search (one half is always sorted) are both examples; the array itself is not sorted.

What does “binary search on the answer” mean and when does it apply?

Instead of searching the input, search the range of possible answers. It applies when (1) the answer is a number in a known range, (2) you can check in polynomial time whether a candidate works, and (3) feasibility is monotone — if x works, every larger (or every smaller) value works too. Minimum pages, Koko bananas and painter's partition fit this mould; each check is a greedy O(n) pass.

Why does low + (high - low) / 2 matter in C++ and Java?

(low + high) can overflow a 32-bit int when both are near 2³¹ - 1, yielding a negative mid and an out-of-bounds read. low + (high - low) / 2 never exceeds high. Python and JavaScript are not affected (arbitrary-precision ints / 64-bit doubles), but write it the same way for habit.

How does the two-pointer method guarantee it does not skip the answer?

When arr[i] + arr[j] < x, every pair (i, j') with j' < j has an even smaller sum, so index i can never be part of a solution — discarding it is safe. The symmetric argument applies when the sum is too large. Each step permanently retires one index, so the loop terminates after at most n - 1 steps and never discards a valid pair.

Explain Floyd's cycle detection and why it finds the repeated element.

Treat each index as a node with one outgoing edge i → arr[i] + 1. A node with two incoming edges is a repeated value; with one start node that nobody points to, the path from it enters a cycle exactly at such a node. Phase 1 (slow 1 step, fast 2 steps) meets inside the cycle; phase 2 (reset slow to the start, both 1 step) meets at the cycle entry because the start-to-entry distance equals the meeting-point-to-entry distance modulo the cycle length. Two variables, O(n) steps, no writes.

Median of two sorted arrays — why search the shorter array?

i1 ranges over 0..n1; the matching i2 = (n1 + n2 + 1) / 2 - i1 must stay in 0..n2. That is guaranteed only when n1 <= n2. Searching the shorter array also gives the better O(log min(n1, n2)) bound and halves the special cases you need to reason about.
